ANAHEIM, Calif. — As Nori Aoki and Lorenzo Cain ran toward each other — and the right-center-field wall — it did not look as if it would end well for the Kansas City Royals outfielders. If Howie Kendrick’s sixth-inning drive were to fall, two runs would surely score, putting the Los Angeles Angels ahead. And if Cain and Aoki ran into each other, that would not be so good either.
So, as Cain, with his 37-inch vertical jump, leapt into the air, Aoki figured he had better take an alternate route.
“Cain’s a bigger guy,” the Japanese-speaking Aoki said through an interpreter, smiling. “Cain goes up top. I should go on the bottom.”
So Aoki went low, turned his head and stuck his glove out toward his backhand. He felt the ball hit it, and then he looked.
“I saw it, and it was barely in there,” said Aoki, who bounced off the wall, held the ball up and then celebrated with Cain as they bounced back to the dugout.
The play kept the Royals in the opener of the American League division series, their bullpen survived several late-inning scares and Mike Moustakas’s solo homer in the 11th inning delivered Kansas City a 3-2 victory.
Just two games
into the Royals’ long-awaited journey into the playoffs, and it has been as head-spinning as Aoki’s catch. After their two stirring late-inning comebacks to beat Oakland on Tuesday in the wild-card playoff, the trip west continued to provide memories.
And not just for Aoki and Cain, who each made other remarkable catches, and Moustakas, who had batted just .212 during the regular season and homered in front of his friends and family. Danny Duffy, another local product, got over his disappointment of being dropped from the rotation for this series by pitching a scoreless inning for the win.
But the most shellshocked of the Royals may have been the All-Star closer Greg Holland, who flew in from Asheville, N.C., after returning home for the birth of his son. Holland arrived in the middle of the game, then retired the Angels in order in the 11th inning to seal the victory.
“I expect it to be tight, competitive and fun,” Cain said of the playoffs, the Royals' first since 1985. “As long as we win, I’m all for it.”
The Angels, in the playoffs for the first time since 2009, arrived with the best record in baseball and the presumptive league most valuable player, center fielder Mike Trout, and two former ones — Albert Pujols and Josh Hamilton.
But the three were hitless in 13 at-bats, including Hamilton’s pop up to third base that ended the game. Hamilton, who played in only one of the last 22 games because of a sore shoulder, did not hit the ball out of the infield and twice left runners in scoring position. Trout and Pujols came up with runners on base in their final three at-bats, but could not deliver a base hit.
The Angels' only runs came on solo homers by catcher Chris Iannetta and third baseman David Freese.
“We just couldn’t get that one hit,” the Angels’ manager, Mike Scioscia, said. “We hit two home runs to keep ourselves in the game, but outside of that, we didn’t really pressure those guys very much.”

Even on a warm evening — it was 93 degrees at game time — each team managed only four hits. But there may have been several others if not for some sterling defensive plays — some by the Angels, but most by the Royals’ outfielders.
Cain leapt high against the outfield wall to take an extra-base hit from Kole Calhoun leading off the bottom of the first, an effort that prompted Royals pitcher Jason Vargas to exhale loudly. In the seventh, Aoki did not look as graceful, tracking a deep fly from C. J. Cron into the corner. Aoki stumbled and lurched, but reached out and grabbed the ball before it hit the warning track.
“Lorenzo Cain and Aoki in right field, that’s where the game was won for Kansas City,” Scioscia said. “Howie hit a bullet with guys in scoring position. C. J. hit a bullet with guys in scoring position. That is what really kept those guys in the game.”
The Angels will turn to Matt Shoemaker, who was 16-4 after just hoping to earn a spot in the bullpen in spring training, against the Royals in Game 2. He will face the Royals’ hard-throwing Yordano Ventura, who will be trying to cover for an already taxed bullpen. Six relievers covered the final seven innings against Oakland, and seven pitched on Thursday — including Kelvin Herrera, who left after five pitches with tightness in his right arm.
But a deep bullpen, playmaking defense and creating havoc on the bases are how the Royals have reached the postseason. What they have not done is hit home runs. They hit only 95 during the regular season, the fewest in the major leagues.
But the belief in the Royals dugout is strong right now. And given the way they played Thursday night, flying all over to take away hits, the possibility of winning a game on a home run by Moustakas was not the biggest leap of all.
Correction: October 3, 2014
An earlier version of this article misstated the status of Royals pitcher Danny Duffy. He was a rookie in 2011, not this season.

10:05 A.M. (Flix) THE DANGEROUS LIVES OF ALTAR BOYS
(2002) In Jeff Stockwell’s screen adaptation of Chris Fuhrman’s novel, directed by Peter Care, the teenage friends Francis Doyle (Emile Hirsch) and Tim Sullivan (Kieran Culkin) cope with the anxieties of education, puberty and first love by writing a series of superhero comics. “The masterstroke of this small, heartfelt directorial debut,” Stephen Holden
wrote in The New York Times
, “is its integration of animated sequences (by Todd McFarlane) in which action-adventure caricatures of the comic book characters parallel or comment on events in the boys’ lives.” Those lives are darkened as the film progresses, most affectingly by a story of familial abuse shared by Francis’s new girlfriend, Margie Flynn (Jena Malone). Jodie Foster plays Sister Assumpta, an especially reviled teacher at the boys’ Roman Catholic school. Mr. Holden wrote: “Ms. Foster, who seems to grow primmer with each film, locates the compassion beneath her character’s grim, authoritarian surface. Like tiny ripples on a pond, her face registers the concerns of a caring surrogate parent committed to practicing an austere form of tough love.”
2 P.M. (FXM) DOUBT
(2008) John Patrick Shanley wrote and directed this film adaptation of his Pulitzer Prize-winning play, “Doubt: A Parable.” Meryl Streep plays Sister Aloysius, a nun in the Bronx who comes to believe that the parish priest, Father Flynn (Philip Seymour Hoffman), has developed an unhealthy interest in the lone black pupil at the parish’s Roman Catholic school. (The story is set in 1964.) “Mr. Shanley has nothing deep to say about the church and its sex scandals,” Manohla Dargis
wrote in The Times
. “His work with the actors is generally fine, though it’s a mystery what he thought Ms. Streep, with her wild eyes and an accent as wide as the Grand Concourse, was doing. Her outsize performance has a whiff of burlesque, but she’s really just operating in a different register from the other actors, who are working in the more naturalistic vein of modern movie realism. She’s a hoot, but she’s also a relief, because, for some of us, worshiping Our Lady of Accents is easier on the soul than doing time in church.”
3 P.M. (Flix) NIXON
(1995) Oliver Stone’s three-hour-plus portrait of the 37th president is less conspiracy-minded than his film “J. F. K.” The movie begins with the young Richard M. Nixon in Yorba Linda, Calif., and ricochets through his college years, his political rise, his vice presidency, his electoral defeats in 1960 and 1962, his secret war in Cambodia, his visit to China and his immersion in the Vietnam War. Having done all that, Janet Maslin
wrote in The Times
, the film “starts snowballing its way to real dramatic power.” Its finale, staged in a White House that the lonely president seems to haunt rather than live in, pictures Nixon as a tragic figure out of Shakespeare. The portrayal of the president by Anthony Hopkins is “overwhelmingly vivid,” Ms. Maslin wrote, and Pat Nixon is “played gracefully and touchingly” by Joan Allen.

8 P.M. (Comedy Central) TOSH.0
Daniel Tosh returns to television with the first new “Tosh.0” episodes since May. This week Mr. Tosh examines back-to-school fashions.
10 P.M. (BBCA) PLANET EARTH: HUMAN PLANET
This is a rebroadcast of the first episode of the series featuring people from around the world who do dangerous, difficult work to get by. The series is organized geographically; this episode is about people who live with, by, and, in some cases, in, the ocean. Spaniards scale dangerous cliffs to collect barnacles; Indonesians hunt sperm whales with hand-held harpoons; Bajau fishermen disappear underwater for minutes at a time without the aid of scuba equipment. “The filmmaking is breathtaking,” Neil Genzlinger
wrote in The Times
, “and, if you think about it too hard, question-inducing. Where exactly is the camera operator standing, and how, to get those shots of the fishermen who pluck their catches from the very top of Victoria Falls in Africa?”
WHAT’S STREAMING NOW
SLEEPY HOLLOW (ABC)
After 250 years of slumber, the former American Colonial soldier Ichabod Crane (Tom Mison) rises from the grave in modern-day New York. His troubles upon awakening include culture shock as well as the headless horseman. The show’s second season premieres on Sept. 22; the first is available now on Hulu (
hulu.com/sleepy-hollow

First he raised water and sewer rates. Then he helped engineer the skimpiest rent increases in the history of rent regulation.
After that came the threats to mandate more investment in energy efficiency. Next was a law to publicly shame landlords who harass tenants.
Almost a year into the administration of Mayor
Bill de Blasio
, many New York City landlords say they are not feeling the love.
“Politically, I’ve never seen a climate more dangerous than I’m facing now,” said Jimmy Silber, co-president of Small Property Owners of New York, a landlord advocacy group.
Mr. de Blasio is a fellow landlord, with tenants in Park Slope, Brooklyn, in
a duplex
that belonged to his deceased mother and in
his family’s townhouse
(while the family lives at Gracie Mansion). But he kept a “worst landlords” watch list while he was the city’s public advocate, and a central promise of his mayoral campaign was to protect low-income tenants and make housing more affordable for the poor and working class.
Ask tenant leaders about the mayor and they say so far so good. Ask rent-regulated landlords and they say they are just bracing themselves for the next hit.
“Where does the city get most of its money?” asked Reshit Gjinovic, who owns a six-unit building in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn. “It comes from landlords and taxes. I hope he wakes up.”
The bad blood is bound to thicken next year when New York’s rent laws come up for renewal and the State Legislature weighs whether to make them stronger, or weaker. The mayor promised before his election that he would join tenant leaders in trying to wrest control of rent regulation from the state so that the city would be able to make rent laws stricter.
But tenant groups regard that effort as a long shot. They are focused instead on extracting at least one victory with the mayor’s help: the repeal of the provision that allows landlords to deregulate an apartment after it becomes vacant and is rented for $2,500 or more.
Mr. Silber said it is expected that the just-elected Republican majority in the State Senate will block those efforts next year, but “there’s always the threat of
Bill de Blasio
getting his way” in the future.
Continue reading the main story
Jaron Benjamin, executive director of the Metropolitan Council on Housing, an affordable housing advocacy group, said of Mr. de Blasio, “Having a mayor that understands the value of protecting rent-regulated housing has the potential to make all the difference.”
Many landlords fault Mr. de Blasio for overlooking the plight of property owners who are having their own difficulties meeting expenses to maintain their buildings as property taxes, fuel, insurance and other costs go up. A big blow came in June, they said, when the Rent Guidelines Board voted for a 1 percent rent increase for one-year leases and 2.75 percent for two-year leases. They were the lowest increases since the city created the board, which regulates nearly one million apartments in the city, in 1969.
Mayor de Blasio had advocated for a rent freeze for leases of one year, a position owners said ignored the board’s own reports showing rising operating costs. But the mayor’s office pointed out that the board’s staff also found that owners’ net income after operating expenses were paid had risen for eight consecutive years, most recently by more than 9 percent.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
Landlords of small buildings said they have it worst and the city should come up with other relief, such as tax credits, to compensate them for keeping a lid on rents. “The administration needs to look at this landlord issue as not a singular group,” said Richard Thorne, who owns a four-family home with two stabilized one-bedroom units in the Chelsea section of Manhattan.
Mr. Thorne said many large landlords can at least make a profit by offsetting losses from their regulated apartments with profits from those that rent at market rate. But some landlords with market-rate units noted that those make little difference in neighborhoods with modest rents.
Mr. Gjinovic said the market rate for his two unregulated apartments in Bay Ridge was no higher than $1,400, well under the $2,500 threshold that landlords in wealthier areas reach to deregulate the units.
This year, for the first time, he said, his building did not generate enough revenue to cover the rising expenses, including higher taxes, insurance and water bills, as well as $31,000 for a new boiler and pointing work.
He said he could not sell even if he wanted to. “Who’s going to come in and buy it if I lose money?” Mr. Gjinovic asked.
The mayor is not altogether unfamiliar with the landlords’ trials. While running for mayor last year, Mr. de Blasio had a simple response to criticism that he had failed to disclose his rental income to the Conflicts of Interest Board: There was no net income to report. His taxes, mortgage interest and depreciation on the property, his campaign said, exceeded revenue from the rent.
Of course, being a landlord is a sideline for Mr. de Blasio, who has been in public office for the last 12 years — as the public advocate and a city councilman before that — and now makes $225,000 a year as mayor.
Landlord groups scoff at Mr. de Blasio the landlord. Some noted that neither the duplex nor the townhome is rent-regulated, so the mayor is not affected by the rent guidelines for which he advocates.
“He can rent a house for $5,000 a month while arguing to not increase rents,” said Jack Freund, executive vice president of the Rent Stabilization Association, a landlord group. “It’s pretty outrageous.” (The exact rent for the townhouse is $4,975 a month.)
Wiley Norvell, a spokesman for Mr. de Blasio, said that “the mayor knows firsthand what it’s like to be an outer-borough homeowner.”
“We’ve worked hard to ease the burden facing tenants, but we also recognize the affordability crisis is hitting all kinds of New Yorkers,” Mr. Norvell said. “That’s why we’re working to help small-building owners lower utility costs and freezing water rates for many seniors.”
Water and sewer rates indeed went up in May by only 3.35 percent, the smallest increase in nine years. But landlords fault Mr. de Blasio for raising them at all after criticizing Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg for raising those rates every year.
Before this year’s elections, Mr. de Blasio urged donors to contribute to state legislative candidates and sent his top strategists to advise on races seeking a Democratic majority in the State Senate. But voters gave the Senate a clear Republican majority, which property owners see as their only defense against a Democratic push for rent-law reform.
Nearly 5,000 stabilized apartments were lost to deregulation through vacancies last year, and tenant leaders regard the vacancy loophole as the single largest threat to affordable housing in the city. But Mr. Silber, of the property owners group that represents mostly buildings of 10 or fewer apartments, said the ability to deregulate an apartment is the “lifeblood” for some owners.
“That one apartment where you can get $2,500, all of a sudden you have an infusion of funds that help the owner make expenses,” he said. Some people in the real estate industry said the uncertainty did not help the mayor’s goal of preserving or building 200,000 affordable units over 10 years, because changes in rent regulation affect property deals.
“The market on all levels is waiting for clarity so they can make decisions,” said Ofer Cohen, president of TerraCHG, a brokerage firm that works in the residential market in Brooklyn. “Without certainty, there’s less activity.”

To promote quick and easy transfers between flights — with a particular focus on those bound for Asia — Helsinki Airport is the host of a pop-up skateboarding invitational from Oct. 12 to 13.
The event will turn the airport into a temporary playground featuring the Finnish skateboarding star Arto Saari, along with the United States skaters Curren Caples and Louie Lopez.
The first skating session on Oct. 12 will be held in Finland’s biggest building: one of Finnair’s aircraft maintenance halls. The session on Oct. 13  is in the terminal building at Helsinki Airport.
More than 250 video entries of skateboarders from over 50 different countries were submitted on the site
#matchmadeinHEL.com
in late September; from this pool, four skaters will be selected and will have skating sessions with Mr. Saari’s crew.
Videos from the sessions will be on Finnair’s
YouTube channel;
Mr. Saari says in one of his videos, “I’ve always had this idea of skating in places where you’re not supposed to skate.”
The invitational follows some
recent news
from Helsinki Airport. To improve connection times between flights, airport management has decided to expand its existing terminal rather than build a separate satellite terminal.
Mari Rouvi, Finnair’s communications manager, said that while Copenhagen airport receives more traffic, Helsinki Airport offers the fastest connections (no more than 35 minutes) to Asia-bound flights, and also the shortest route to Asia from the West.
Finnair has a goal of doubling the revenues of its Asian traffic by 2020 and the airport is preparing to accommodate 20 million passengers per year by that year.

Kerry Recalls Vietnam as U.S. Thaws Cuba Policy
1:12
pm ET
1:12
pm ET
Alan Rappeport
Secretary of State John Kerry, who once fought in Vietnam, said that American efforts to ease relations with Cuba could parallel the path that the United States had  traveled with the Vietnamese government since that war ended.
“Beginning more than twenty years ago, I have seen first hand as three presidents — one Republican and two Democrats — have undertaken a similar effort to change the United States’ relationship with Vietnam. It wasn’t easy,” Mr. Kerry said. “It isn’t complete still today. But it had to start somewhere, and it has worked.”
Mr. Kerry said that, as with Vietnam, easing relations with Cuba will take time, energy and resources. However, he argued that the costs of trying to turn the tide were lower than the risks associated with “remaining stuck in an ideological cement of our own making.”

The hundreds of children who recently arrived in New York City from Central America have encountered a justice system that appears more forgiving than many faced by their counterparts elsewhere. In an immigration courtroom in Lower Manhattan, they have often met judges who have
steered them
through the legal process with a gentle hand.
But challenges mount outside the courtroom, beginning with the seemingly mundane obligations of registering for school and securing health care. Many young immigrants remain unaware of the available support or are afraid to seek it out.
In response, the city
announced on Tuesday
that it would help bring those services to children by placing representatives at federal immigration court, a move that officials called the first of its kind in the city.
As more and more children face deportation hearings under an accelerated court process meant to deal with the influx of unaccompanied minors, health and education officials have begun offering advice just outside the courtroom, closing a gap that officials say has left children in limbo.
“Connecting these vulnerable children to educational, health and social services is vital to helping our families and communities gain stability,” Mayor
Bill de Blasio
said in a statement, calling the city’s response “a more humanitarian approach.”
At a hearing on Tuesday morning before two State Assembly committees, the city’s commissioner for immigrant affairs, Nisha Agarwal, described the immigration court as an opportune place to reach children before they disappear into their communities, where they may lack the resources to handle everyday logistical challenges.
The city also plans to set up weekend workshops at public schools with large immigrant populations so that representatives can advise families on matters from mental health services to vaccinations.
“Rather than creating a new program, how do you link this special population to the existing programs that are already there?” Ms. Agarwal said.
By redistributing staff members who are already working on community outreach, she added, the program would not create any additional cost for the city.
State politicians and those advocating immigration rights called the plan an unprecedented example of collaboration between a city and federal court system. They said they worried that some courts in other parts of the country were trampling on due process as they sped up deportation proceedings, a cornerstone of the Obama administration’s plan to accelerate the legal process for newly arrived children.
Addressing Ms. Agarwal at the hearing on Tuesday, Assemblyman Marcos A. Crespo said, “Whereas other communities have taken a staunch opposition to even indulging the needs here, you guys have done quite the opposite.”
About 1,350 unaccompanied minors settled with family members or other sponsors in New York City in the first seven months of this year, according to the Office of Refugee Resettlement, a federal agency.
While immigrant children have registered for public school in New York City with relative ease, some have not known how to enroll in
Child Health Plus
, a public health insurance system, lawyers said.

Others have had trouble proving that they were vaccinated when they crossed the border, or have had to depend on overtaxed pro bono lawyers to steer them to doctors.
Even some fledgling volunteer lawyers do not know how to gather the basic paperwork that their clients need to receive city services, supporters say.
“Getting kids in contact with the schools is frankly the second most urgent step after giving them a lawyer,” said Camille Mackler, director of legal initiatives at the
New York Immigration Coalition
. “We need to make sure kids have access to services because they won’t know what they’re entitled to.”
Others urged the city to expand its support so that representatives can also guide children who are arriving at court in Lower Manhattan from counties on Long Island and in the Hudson Valley.
Lenni Benson, director of the New York Law School
Safe Passage Project
, recalled a city representative recently offering to search for the right phone number on Google when a child from upstate asked how to register for school.
“Maybe they could do a little bit more,” Ms. Benson said, referring to the representative.
As for school registration requirements around the state, she added, “These benign requirements are not benign.”

★ Americanafest NYC
(Friday through Sunday) This weeklong festival, running in conjunction with Lincoln Center Out of Doors, concludes this weekend with a few heavy-hitters. On Friday at 7:30 p.m., Cassandra Wilson celebrates the 20th anniversary of “Blue Light ’Til Dawn,” an album that established Ms. Wilson as an expressive jazz singer with one foot planted in the loam of American folk and roots music; it has aged gracefully and exerted a broad influence, like Ms. Wilson herself. On Saturday at 1:30 p.m., the Old 97’s, alternative-country torchbearers since the early 1990s who released the raucous album “Most Messed Up” in April, will join the Devil Makes Three and John Fullbright for an afternoon performance at Hearst Plaza. That night, at 6 p.m., Rosanne Cash, the eminently cool daughter of Johnny Cash and a skilled singer-songwriter in her own right, will perform with the Lone Bellow and Buddy Miller & Jim Lauderdale. On Ms. Cash’s latest release, “The River and the Thread,” which arrived in January, she nudged some gospel and rock into her twangy flavor. On Sunday at 5 p.m., the Daptone Records mainstay Charles Bradley, 65, performs with his Extraordinaires. Mr. Bradley resurrects the electric communality of 1970s funk and soul and, when performing live, he becomes a crooning, celebratory force. They share the stage with St. Paul & the Broken Bones, Bobby Patterson and Music Maker Blues Revue. These concerts will be streamed live at
watch.lincolncenter.org
. All shows are at Damrosch Park, Lincoln Center (except the Old 97’s concert, which is at Lincoln Center’s Hearst Plaza), 212-721-6500,
lcoutofdoors.org
; free. (Nate Chinen and Stacey Anderson)
★ Tori Amos
(Tuesday and Wednesday) This alt-pop earth mother let her classical piano chops flourish on “Unrepentant Geraldines,” her most recent studio album. In addition to contemplations on wayward love and pop culture, she weaves tales around mortality, maturity and motherhood, sharing a duet (“Promise”) with her teenage daughter, Tash. The new album arrived on the heels of Ms. Amos’s fantastical musical, “The Light Princess,” which recently had an extended run at the Royal National Theater in London. Don’t be surprised if she pulls from that whimsical songbook in concert. With Trevor Moss & Hannah-Lou. At 8 p.m., Beacon Theater, 2124 Broadway, at 74th Street, 800-745-3000,
beacontheatrenyc.com
; $42.50 to $77.50. (Anderson)
Baauer
(Sunday) The Brooklyn electronic dance music D.J.-producer behind the “Harlem Shake,” Baauer took home the top EDM song trophy for that hit at the 2013 Billboard Music Awards. He has also remixed Nero’s “Won’t You (Be There)" and No Doubt’s “Settle Down,” and just released a futuristic, aptly named new single, “Clang.” He will be one of the D.J.s opening for Boys Noize this weekend. At 4 p.m., Governors Beach Club, Governors Island,
pachanyc.com
; $50. (Anderson)

★ Celebrate Brooklyn: St. Vincent
(Saturday) The restless multi-instrumentalist Annie Clark, who performs as St. Vincent, is an inquisitive songwriter, a versatile singer and a sharp explorer of femininity within punk- and baroque-laced aggression. Her terrific recent self-titled album ratchets up the brassy art-rock approach of “Love This Giant,” her joint album with David Byrne, by adding skittish, synthesized dystopic arrangements and cutting lyrics. She closes the Celebrate Brooklyn! concert series with San Fermin. At 7:30 p.m., Prospect Park Bandshell, Prospect Park West and Ninth Street, Park Slope, Brooklyn,
bricartsmedia.org
; free. (Anderson)
The Cult
(Tuesday) These heavy metal and punk mercenaries from Bradford, England, released their ninth studio album, “Choice of Weapon,” two years ago. The first single, the brawny and slightly brainless “For the Animals,” favored arena rock decadence over the arty irascibility that helped them make their name in the 1980s. At 8 p.m., the Paramount, 370 New York Avenue, Huntington, N.Y., 800-745-3000,
paramountny.com
; $37.50 to $75. (Anderson)
Infected Mushroom
(Friday) Ratcheting, propulsive groans and aggressive synthetic beats align this Israeli psychedelic-trance duo closer to industrial rock than electronic dance music. Their complex live shows are spectacles worthy of full gawping. They perform with a live band as part of the Girls and Boys dance party. At 9 p.m., Webster Hall, 125 East 11th Street, East Village, 866-777-8932,
websterhall.com/events
; $30 and $35. (Anderson)
Kings of Leon
(Wednesday) Still hitting the road in support of their nearly year-old sixth studio album, “Mechanical Bull,” Kings of Leon are seasoned pros at filling arenas with their brand of Southern rock. They’re also a rather photogenic family band — Caleb, Jared and Nathan Followill are brothers, and Matthew is their cousin — best known for their megahits “Lose Somebody” and “Sex on Fire.” With Young the Giant and Kongos. At 7 p.m., Nikon at Jones Beach Theater, Wantagh, N.Y., 800-745-3000,
jonesbeach.com
; $49.50 to $75.50. (Anderson)
Mad Decent Block Party with Diplo and Dillon Francis
(Saturday) The seemingly omnipotent D.J.-producer Diplo helms the electro-heavy record label Mad Decent, spearheads the reggae-dance project Major Lazer, spins hip-hop-tinged sets in the most mammoth halls and produces for the likes of M.I.A. and Beyoncé. Fittingly, he headlines this tour of his label’s artists and associated acts. Mr. Francis, one of the leading spinners of moombahcore — that onomatopoeic hybrid of house, reggae and drummy techno — will also perform, as well as Flosstradamus, Grandtheft and others. At 3 p.m., MCU Park, 1904 Surf Avenue, at West 17th Street, Coney Island, Brooklyn, 800-745-3000,
maddecentblockparty.com
; $43.50. (Anderson)
Modest Mouse
(Saturday) After spending over a decade in the warm embrace of niche indie-rock worship, and occasionally mocking sunsets and picnics in its droll lyrics, Modest Mouse broke into the mainstream with a vengeance via “Float On,” from its excellent 2004 album, “Good News for People Who Love Bad News.” The group is rumored to be working on the follow-up to its last release, “No One’s First and You’re Next,” an EP from 2009. With Brand New. At 6:30 p.m., Forest Hills Stadium, 1 Tennis Place, at Burns Street, Forest Hills, Queens,
foresthillsstadium.com
,
ticketfly.com
; $49.50 to $59.50. (Anderson)

MoMA Nights: Frankie Cosmos
(Thursday) A former poetry student at New York University, and the daughter of the actors Phoebe Cates and Kevin Kline, the young Greta Kline constructs preternaturally poised, lo-fi folk-pop with thoughtful verses and echoing vocals. She leads the band Frankie Cosmos, which released its debut, “Zentropy,” in the spring; the art set is already keen to claim her, as evidenced by this MoMA set. At 5:30 p.m., Museum of Modern Art, 212-708-9400,
moma.org
; free, with museum admission: $25, $18 for 65+, $14 for students, free for those 16 and younger. (Anderson)
★ Nellie McKay
(Friday and Saturday) Although New York’s cabaret season quiets down somewhat during August, the scene is still fairly lively. Nellie McKay, the curly-haired blond deconstructionist, continues her run at 54 Below in her new show, “A Girl Named Bill,” a musical biography of the jazz pianist, saxophonist and bandleader Billy Tipton, who died in 1989. After his death, Tipton was discovered to have been born a woman. At 8 p.m., 254 West 54th Street, Manhattan, 646-476-3551,
54below.com
; $50 to $85 cover in advance, $5 extra at the door, with a $25 minimum. Other highlights this month: For three Sundays, starting Aug. 17, 54 Below is presenting two performances a night of its first New York Cabaret Festival, which features a different lineup of 12 performers, some well-known, others obscure, for each show. At Birdland, the 15th annual celebration of Django Reinhardt, the great French guitarist of Romany heritage, continues through Sunday. The isolating effects of human development are causing a sharp decline in genetic diversity among mountain lions in Southern California, a new study says.
Researchers from the University of California, Davis, collected DNA samples from more than 350 mountain lions throughout California and found that animals separated by little more than a highway have far less genetic material in common than they did just 80 years ago, suggesting that there is far less interbreeding among populations.
Pumas in the Santa Ana Mountains — effectively fenced in by Interstate 15 to the east, the Pacific Ocean to the west and Los Angeles to the north — displayed lower genetic diversity than those from nearly any other region in the state. So severe is their isolation that the Santa Ana pumas have more in common genetically with lions 400 miles to the north than their neighbors in the Santa Monica Mountains.
Tests revealed that the decline in diversity had taken place “within four to six mountain lion generations,” said Holly Ernest, lead author of
the study
in PLOS One. “So we know that this is happening on a recent time scale” and is a likely result of human development rather than natural separation from other mountain lions.
“Genetically diverse populations are better able to handle whatever nature or humans throw at them, like climate change or disease,” said Dr. Ernest, a geneticist now at the University of Wyoming. “If mountain lions lose that genetic diversity, they lose that resilience.”

The surest sign that international publishers were caught off guard when the French novelist Patrick Modiano won this year’s Nobel literature prize was that few of his books were available in translation. Many people in France were also surprised, but for a different reason. Unlike most of that country’s intellectuals, Modiano has never sought celebrity. Indeed, this 69-year-old man seems as shy and withdrawn today as he was at 23, when his first novel was published.
This is apparent in the stuttering responses he offers in his rare interviews. It is still more evident in the elusive, introspective quality of his writing. His novels have been described as literary detective stories, yet the mysteries he examines are never fully solved, so he keeps returning to them. “I always have the impression that I write the same book, which means it’s already 45 years that I’ve been writing the same book,” he remarked when informed of his Nobel Prize.
The three novellas in “Suspended Sentences” first appeared in France between 1988 and 1993. With another author, they might be considered examples of earlier work, but not so with Modiano. Vividly translated by Mark Polizzotti, they are as good a place as any to enter the long, slow-moving river of Modiano’s fiction.
The Swedish Academy honored him “for the art of memory with which he has evoked the most ungraspable human destinies and uncovered the life-world of the occupation.” But if “memory” and “occupation” are useful tags for his writing, it is another word — “father” — that provides the real key to his unfinished exploration of the German occupation of France. In his late teens, Modiano deduced that his Jewish-Italian father, Albert, spent the war years as a black marketeer associated with the notorious and brutal Rue Lauriston gang, also known as the French Gestapo. And since his father revealed nothing before his death in 1977, not even who ordered his release from a Jewish detention center in Paris in 1943, Modiano became obsessed with knowing more.
Continue reading the main story
His first novel, “La Place de l’Étoile,” published in 1968 and still not translated into English, is arguably his most explosive. As if directly confronting his father, Modiano’s narrator, Raphaël Schlemilovitch, is an amoral Jew who hangs out with the most renowned French collaborators. Modiano’s father was outraged, and the two became even more estranged.
In most of Modiano’s other books, in which the occupation is more of a past trauma than a continuing tragedy, he sets out to fill the gaps of memory, to discover what really happened. In the 1997 novel “Dora Bruder,” for example, he tries to unravel the mystery of why a 15-year-old Jewish girl fled the safety of a convent in late 1941, only to be recorded months later on a train carrying Jews to Auschwitz.
In the novellas translated now in “Suspended Sentences,” the narrator seems inseparable from Modiano, even calling himself Patoche, a nickname for Patrick. He remembers people, events, buildings and streets from the 1950s and ’60s and then, writing years later, excavates an account of the occupation. Yet where real life gives way to fiction remains unclear.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
In “Afterimage,” the 19-year-old narrator meets a middle-aged Jewish-Italian photographer, Francis Jansen, who was arrested during the occupation and released at the request of the Italian Consulate. Befriended by Robert Capa, he worked for some time for the Magnum agency (no Jansen is listed as having been a member of Magnum), but he now plans to abandon photography and leave France. The narrator offers to catalog his prints. “I had taken on this job because I refused to accept that people and things could disappear without a trace,” he writes, as if explaining Modiano’s entire literary mission. He also meets Jansen’s mistress and friends, but when he later writes about them, he laments that “so many proofs and witnesses can disappear in 30 years.”
In the title novella, set in 1955, Patoche and his younger brother are lodged with three women outside Paris while their actress mother is touring and their father is traveling. The house has mysterious visitors, and one evening Patoche hears one say: “Andrée was part of the Rue Lauriston gang.” At the time, this means nothing to him, but: “Subsequently, I again overheard the name in their conversation and I became used to the sound of it. A few years later, I heard it in the mouth of my father, but I didn’t know that ‘the Rue Lauriston gang’ would haunt me for such a long time.”
He describes his father’s detention in the Magasins Généraux on the Quai de la Gare, where looted Jewish belongings were sorted for shipment to Germany. “One night someone showed up in an automobile at the Quai de la Gare and had my father released. I imagined — rightly or wrongly — that it was a certain Louis Pagnon, whom they called ‘Eddy’ and who was shot after the Liberation with members of the Rue Lauriston gang, to which he belonged.”
Patoche’s childhood account also ends abruptly. During his lunch break from school, he finds the women’s house empty. Puzzled, he and his brother go for a walk and return to find the police searching the house. They are told that “something very serious” has happened. “And my brother and I, we pretended to play in the garden, waiting for someone to come collect us.” Only later does he understand that the women and their visitors were trafficking in stolen goods.
In the final novella, “Flowers of Ruin,” the narrator returns to the Left Bank of the 1960s, where, while investigating the double suicide of a young couple that took place in 1933, he finds an old newspaper account suggesting that they had been out on the town just beforehand. Ever the sleuth, he discovers a house near Paris with an elevator “lined with red velvet,” which the dying woman had described. Quite separately, he meets an enigmatic man, some 20 years his senior, who goes by the names of Pacheco and Philippe de Bellune. More newspaper research reveals that someone with those names was a collaborator during the occupation and either died in Dachau or was summoned to appear in court after the war. The man known to the narrator then disappears.
Like scattered memories, stories come and go, some connected, others not. One tells of a Sylviane, who married a penniless aristocrat and ended up as mistress to Pagnon, the gangster who may have freed the narrator’s father from internment. “When my father left the Magasins Généraux, I wonder what route he took in the blackout. He must have felt dumbfounded at having been spared.”
Written several years apart, these novellas fit neatly into Modiano’s “same book,” where the shadowy figures and dark streets of postwar Paris are forever scoured for secrets of an occupation most of the French prefer to forget. “Maybe someday,” the author writes in “After­image,” “I’ll manage to break through that layer of silence and amnesia.” He seems certain to keep trying.
SUSPENDED SENTENCES
Three Novellas
By Patrick Modiano
Translated by Mark Polizzotti
213 pp. Yale University Press. Paper, $16.

For over a year, we’ve been working on
PourOver.js
and
Tamper
, two of the internal libraries behind the
Red Carpet Project
,
Faces of Breast Cancer
and
High-Rise reader stories
, among others.
Today, you can find both on
GitHub
:
PourOver.js: a library for filtering, paging, updating and sorting collections of data in the browser
Tamper: a protocol for serializing and compressing categorical data
Both projects have a full set of documentation, and PourOver ships with a series of examples that
cover the basics
. There’s also a
companion post
on the OpenNews Source blog detailing how the projects evolved.
We wanted to introduce the projects here with some examples of cool things they’ll allow you to do:
1)
You can chain filters with Boolean operations.
This composition won’t require a full recalculation. It will only take the cost of unioning, intersecting or differencing the filters’ indices. You can take a color, size and shape filter and use them to find all big shapes that are red or blue but not square:
color_match_r = collection.filters.color.getFn(
"red"
) 
 color_match_b = collection.filters.color.getFn(
"blue"
) 
 size_match = collection.filters.size.getFn(
"big"
) 
 shape_match = collection.filters.shape.getFn(
"square"
) 
 big_red_non_squares = color_match_r
.or
(color_match_b)
.and
(size_match)
.not
(shape_match)
2)
PourOver allows you to mix pure and stateful queries.
If you want pure queries, you can have pure queries. Filters will not remember their last
getFn
.
color_match = collection.filters.color.getFn(
"red"
)
  color_match.current_query
// >> undefined
If you want stateful queries, the filter will remember your last
query
.
color_match.query(
“red”
)
  color_match.current_query
// >> [MatchSet of “red” things]
3)
PourOver allows you to easily make a view, storing your current page as well as the last query.
This view will automatically update when items are updated in, added to, or removed from the collection.
view = new PourOver.view(
“my_view”
,collection,{page_size: 1})
  view.page(1)
// pages one to the right
collection.addItems(new_items)
// view stays paged to the item you were previously on, updating the page if necessary. Also if new items match the currently selected filters, they will automatically be added to the view’s current items.
4)
Tamper can take the categorical data for 10,000 photos and represent it in just 1KB:
gist.github.com/bkoski/10779733#file-gistfile1-json
We’re looking forward to seeing how these libraries are useful to you. You’re welcome to open an issue or pull request on GitHub; you can also write to us directly at
erik.hinton@nytimes.com
or
bkoski@nytimes.com
. Since these libraries are in active use both externally and internally, they will continue to evolve: we’ll post news of updates and major releases right here on Open.

HOYLAKE, England — On the first leg of Gary Woodland’s British Open odyssey, he glanced out the airplane porthole in time to see a baggage handler at Kansas City International Airport haul his golf bag out of a cart, drop it on the tarmac and fling another suitcase on top of it. The sight of the tools of his trade being treated with such little care made Woodland so agitated that his fiancée told him to turn away from the window.
After an excruciatingly tight connection in Chicago, Woodland arrived in Manchester, England, alas, without his clubs or clothes. “Seeing them throw the bags around and then them not showing up, it was definitely a little more stressful than it needed to be,” Woodland said.
For the globe-trotting golfer, mishandled clubs are an occupational hazard. According to
an air transport industry report
, United States carriers had 3.22 mishandled bags per 1,000 passengers last year, while European airlines had nine mishandled bags per 1,000 passengers. No wonder, then, that there are caddies who operate a shuttle service for players’ golf bags, driving them from one tour stop to the next in a trailer for a fee.
There are players who opt to send their clubs to a tournament site by express delivery so that they arrive before the players do. And then there are the fortunate few who can afford the five-figure fee for renting a private jet for overseas travel. That category may soon include Rory McIlroy of Northern Ireland, this year’s 54-hole tournament leader, whose golf bag was missing after a flight last month from Newark to Dublin. He hopes he does not have to travel on that airline’s planes again.
“I’m working on getting my own,” he said with a smile.
For golfers, whose success is predicated on acting only after a careful consideration of the odds, there is no greater leap of faith than entrusting their golf bags to a network of strangers.
The golfers’ stress level is heightened this time every year because the British Open brings into play London’s Heathrow Airport, which Hunter Mahan’s caddie, John Wood, described as “the Bermuda Triangle for bags.”
Continue reading the main story
On the advice of his caddie, Woodland bypassed London, “and they still didn’t make it,” he said of his clubs. Allowing time for any mishandled bags to catch up was also a factor in Woodland’s decision to move his travel plans up a day.
“If I had come over on Monday and they didn’t get there Monday and they didn’t show up until Tuesday, that makes it a little difficult,” he said.
Woodland added: “It was tough having no clothes, no clubs. I couldn’t really do anything. But because we came over a little early, the stressful part was waiting Monday morning for them to arrive.”
Woodland said his bags had been mishandled once before, on a 984-mile flight in 2008 from Orlando, Fla., to Dallas, where he was headed to try to qualify for the PGA Tour. “They didn’t show up for a day and a half,” he said. “I was getting really worried.”
Continue reading the main story
This time, Woodland was reunited with his bags around noon Monday, after a delay of about 27 hours. He should consider himself fortunate.
In 2009, Mahan said, he traveled through Heathrow for the British Open at Turnberry in Scotland. He arrived on the Monday before the tournament. His bags did not show up until less than 24 hours before his Thursday round.
Golfers can travel 25 to 30 times a year, including long-haul flights, so they learn quickly to become as methodical about dealing with a lost bag as they are with a lost ball during a round.
“You find your baggage-claim ticket and start that process,” Mahan said. “You find out when the next flight is coming in from your previous destination, and that makes you a little at ease.”
Mahan’s next stop, after the baggage-handling office at Heathrow, was the Ping trailer, a mobile pro shop that is at most tournament sites. The company built him a new set of clubs based on his specifications. Mahan borrowed a bag, which stood out because it did not have his name or sponsors stitched across the front. He also had to buy golf shoes and casual shoes, he said, because all he had were the flip-flops he had worn for the flight, having packed his other footwear in his golf bag to save room in his suitcase.
Mahan missed the cut at Turnberry. Not coincidentally, he said he had avoided all the London airports since. Last week, instead of flying directly to Heathrow from Dallas, where he is based, and connecting on a short-hop flight, Mahan flew to Manchester through Atlanta.
“It’s a terrible feeling when your clubs don’t make it,” Mahan said. “You feel desperation, for sure. You wonder, ‘Are the clubs gone forever?’ ”
On occasion, the answer is yes.
In 2001, Marc Leishman made his first overseas trip, from his native Australia to San Diego for the Junior World Golf Championships. Leishman, then 17, surrendered his golf bag to a ticket agent at the check-in counter, and that was the last he saw of it.
Leishman’s clubs have been mishandled a few times since, including twice in Malaysia before a tour event in Kuala Lumpur. “So that’s a trend with that tournament,” he said.
Two years ago, Leishman said, he traveled there from his home base in Virginia Beach through New York and London using two airlines. It was a high-risk strategy, and sure enough, when Leishman landed in Kuala Lumpur, his Titleist clubs were nowhere to be seen. With no Titleist trailer on site, Leishman was like a musician expected to perform without his instrument.
The 6-foot-2 Leishman borrowed Titleist clubs from the American Charley Hoffman, who is two inches shorter, because Hoffman had brought two sets. Leishman practiced with Hoffman’s equipment on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.
Leishman was set to tee off before 10 a.m. for his first round. “I got a call from reception in my hotel lobby at around 5 a.m. letting me know my clubs were there,” he said. Smiling, Leishman added: “They arrived on my birthday. So that was a nice present.”
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
Balls are lost during tournaments with spotters tracking them. So why should bags be any different?
“There’s nothing you can really do about misplaced luggage,” Leishman said. “It’s bound to happen when you travel as much as we do.”
He added: “We’re lucky. We don’t have to buy new clubs if ours go missing.” Missing clubs are replaced by players’ sponsors.
Clothes are another story. As Henrik Stenson traveled to Manchester last week through Copenhagen, his golf bag made it, but his suitcase did not. He was surprised, he said, because as long as he avoided certain airports, he usually encountered no problems with mishandled baggage.
“Heathrow’s a dangerous place,” Stenson said, adding that Heathrow and Charles de Gaulle, outside Paris, were “the best airports if you want to lose your clubs.”
Faced with the prospect of practicing in clothes bought in the pro shop or in town, Stenson, a stylish Swede, opted for the outfit he had worn on the plane. “I played in shorts the first two days,” he said, “which was lovely.”
Stenson would rather have his suitcase mishandled than his golf bag. In 2009, he stripped down to his briefs to hit a shot out of the mud, so there was no reason to doubt Stenson when he said, “I can play in my underwear.”

It is hard, even knowing just a few facts about Teresa of Ávila, not to fall in love with her. This 16th-century Spanish mystic, saint and doctor of the church could sigh over her own limitations with the precision, earthiness and wit of a born writer. “I could be bribed by a sardine,” she once wrote. Nor did she muffle her sighs over the sisters in her care. “Believe me,” she wrote, “I fear an unhappy nun more than many devils.”
The French psychoanalyst and literary critic Julia Kristeva has not been immune to the charms of this holy woman. She has put Teresa on the couch before (most recently in
“Hatred and Forgiveness”
), and in “Teresa, My Love,” she, or rather her alter ego, the clinical psychologist Sylvia Leclercq, analyzes Teresa and her historical, spiritual and sexual significance.
This book is billed as a novel, but there’s not much story here. Sylvia, a restless sleeper, picks up Teresa’s writings by chance and decides to spend her “submarine nights” reading and researching her new love. Sylvia sees some patients, engages in some romance and travels to Ávila. She’s a somewhat rickety device — more docent than protagonist — through which Ms. Kristeva presents a mix of biography, history, theorizing and even a three-act play. Yet the pieces work together to create a kind of wisdom literature for what Ms. Kristeva likes to call the third millennium.
Descended on her father’s side from Jewish converts to Christianity, this girl who grew up to have raptures was the very pretty daughter of a woman who loved to read novels, a 16th-century Emma Bovary. Her mother passed that love on to her daughter, who might herself have become a thwarted dreamer like Emma, save for a thirst for glory and independence. At 7, Teresa persuaded her brother Rodrigo to run away to “the land of the Moors,” so they could be martyrs. At 21, she ran away again, despite her father’s wishes, to the Carmelites, partly to avoid an unwanted marriage, partly to heed a call.
Sylvia reads Teresa as a woman who needed a Father to love her without judging her for her passions, and a woman who needed to be one with the Son to assure herself she was not solely female, because to be female meant to be sentenced to motherhood. Teresa is also considered, not as explicitly, an exemplar of the feminine genius that Ms. Kristeva has contemplated in books on
Hannah Arendt
, Melanie Klein and
Colette
. Teresa did not imprison herself in an interior castle of mysticism but reformed an order and founded 17 monasteries, traveling all over Spain. In Ms. Kristeva’s interpretation, Teresa isn’t “the patron saint of hysteria,” as Freud’s mentor
Josef Breuer called her
, but the patron saint of passionate pragmatics.
Why Teresa again and why now? “What’s left of that universe of faith and love, what’s left of the windmills?” Sylvia Leclercq asks. “Chimeras, TV soap operas for avid women and their partners. Or God’s madmen, the suicide bombers, who pretend not to realize that he (the Almighty, the Master, the One and Only, the True, the Beyond) has mutated into pure spectacle, and twist their alleged faith into murderous nihilism.” Teresa’s life and her writings could be one antidote to this malaise, because, according to Sylvia/Ms. Kristeva, she “ventures as far as possible along the route that beckons the person who doesn’t give up on believing, the person who talks as a way of sharing, and who loves in order to act.”
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
Does Ms. Kristeva really need nearly 600 pages to expound on the reading she has given the saint elsewhere? At many points, especially in its breathless description and redescription of Teresa’s divine union — a song, like the Song of Songs, that many spiritual seekers might find hard to make their own — Ms. Kristeva’s excess doesn’t lead to illuminating insight. Lovers do run on, Sylvia says, their talk meaningful only to each other, and some readers may experience the book as just that kind of chatter.
“Teresa, My Love” is perhaps strongest when Ms. Kristeva sets her characters in dialogue, particularly a three-act play in which Teresa, on her deathbed, converses with figures like her confessor and friend John of the Cross. Here, Ms. Kristeva’s affection for her subject finds effortless expression in a vibrant and persuasive imagining of Teresa as she might have sounded off the page. Her ebullient exegesis will probably most delight those who think that faith and love need more spokesmen and spokeswomen than just Pope Francis — and more than just believers to speak of them.
Ms. Kristeva’s book may also be particularly appreciated by readers seeking feminist Augustines but who are unfulfilled by contemporary confessions of female wandering that can seem to radiate more self-regard than spiritual wisdom. Those readers will have to tolerate more than a little of what one of Sylvia’s friends calls “Freudian-Lacanian mumbo-jumbo,” but they may also take that mumbo-jumbo over E. L. James any day.
In the end, Ms. Kristeva’s aim is a simple one: Through reconsidering the life of this saint, she is calling those of us “trapped between secularism and fundamentalism” to reconsider what we think we know about love. More specifically, she asks us to rethink our Western resistance to the idealism and loss of self that love involves. Teresa wrote that God “doesn’t give himself but to those who give themselves entirely to him,” and love itself, Ms. Kristeva seems to suggest, might need us to lay down the arms that we have been fashioning since, she argues, Cervantes taught us to snicker at knights errant.
Because Ms. Kristeva is suggesting such a very simple thing, it may be easy to mock her. But at a moment when many seem to think desire is at its most liberated when it’s at its most emotionally detached, we may need a radically simple reminder that the body can be conversant with the soul. And if Ms. Kristeva’s exhortation remains just that — an exhortation, without directions for implementation — that may be the point. As her alter ego says of her efforts, “But that’s also a part of my role: to plant a seed for later, or never.” Frustrating, perhaps, but as her fellow psychoanalyst Adam Phillips might say, sometimes frustration is more productive than we think.
TERESA, MY LOVE
An Imagined Life of the Saint of Avila
By Julia Kristeva
Translated by Lorna Scott Fox. 630 pages. Columbia University Press. $35.

An old hardcover copy of “The Escoffier Cook Book” sits in the library of The New York Times, battered and dog-eared, classified on its front endpaper by someone with exquisite penmanship as a book to be shelved amid titles dedicated to “Foreign Foods.”
It is hard to find. But I have put in my hours, like Hermione Granger in the library at Hogwarts. I know that the spine of “The Escoffier Cook Book,” which faces the reader on the shelf, has fallen off and been replaced with one belonging to “Cooking a La Ritz,” by Louis Diat. I know where it is.
The first few pages of the book are missing, along with the publisher’s information, but the embossed front cover is identical to 1941 editions. It is anyway an old title, and has been hard-used.
Someone — Craig Claiborne, perhaps, who started as food editor of The Times in 1957 and held the position until the 1980s, but more probably a hardworking subeditor or news assistant — made notes here and there in the text. To marinate, he or she underscored in the glossary, means “to soak or steep the product in a prepared sauce or liquid
prior to cooking it.
” The descriptions of bordelaise sauce and chasseur sauce in the section on “The Small Brown Sauces” received dismissive X’s. Montpelier butter, a recipe in the chapter devoted to compound butters, got an enthusiastic check mark.
The book makes for fascinating browsing. I like to read it in the quiet of early evening. Who knows where inspiration is born? A series of words on a page, a stunning picture, a dish in a restaurant, a meal at a friend’s, a smell on a side street and all of a sudden you have to cook that, right now, or else pleasure will have been averted and an opportunity lost. I look for those moments whenever darkness looms.
“
Milanaise Spring Lamb Chops
,” reads a five-line recipe on Page 465. You cook the lamb chops as you might veal chops — dredged in beaten egg, then a mixture of bread crumbs and Parmesan cheese, and sauté them in clarified butter. Standard stuff.
But then: “Arrange them in a circle and, in their midst, put a garnish ‘à la milanaise.’ ” And what is that? Escoffier tells us on another page: “Cooked macaroni, seasoned with salt, pepper and nutmeg, and combined with butter, grated Gruyère and Parmesan cheeses, and very red tomato purée, and combined with a julienne of very lean cooked ham, tongue, mushrooms and truffles, heated in Madeira.”
That had to be made right away. Maybe not with truffles. (Maybe at your house.) Probably not with tongue. (Tongues are large, and the leftovers a bear.) But all the rest — immediately. The dish sounded like
exquisite macaroni and cheese
, nursery food for fancy people, a “garnish” that would be much more than decoration or embellishment.
And it was: rich and luxurious and sweetly fantastic in the offing, just the thing to accompany the lamb. Except: If I’m frying lamb chops, even on a weekend night, I’m not cooking pasta alongside it as “garnish” or anything else. Too complicated from the point of view of the space-time continuum. So I roasted a rack of lamb instead, coated in bread crumbs and grated Parmesan, to achieve similar textures and tastes, without the stress or crowded stovetop. The combination turned out to be outstanding, a last formal nod to the vernal season before summer really kicks in, a show-off dinner-party meal of little compare.
Some things to consider. First, you could omit the lamb and double the recipe for the macaroni to make a meal on its own. Macaroni Milanaise punches hard for its weight in matters of flavor (and calories). Second, you could omit the pasta and eat the lamb as you might its fried cousin at a restaurant in Milan, with a bright salad. The fresh bread crumbs provide a great deal of crunch per munch, while the interior of the meat remains rosy and sweet. Simply tent the exterior of the roast with foil if during the final few minutes of cooking the crust threatens to darken too much.
This is foreign food at its best.

:

SAN ANTONIO — Bob McAdoo, with his graceful, high-arcing jumper, was a rarity for an N.B.A. big man. At 6 feet 9 inches, he could pull shot blockers like Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Artis Gilmore and Bob Lanier out near the top of the key and shoot over them or drive past them. Three times, McAdoo led the league in scoring, and in 1975, he was named the N.B.A.’s most valuable player.
But when the N.B.A. instituted the 3-point line midway through his career, McAdoo did not venture there. He made just three 3-point shots in seven seasons.
“It was a strain for most of us,” McAdoo said. “When I did shoot it, it was a desperation shot.”
So as McAdoo sits on the bench of the
Miami Heat
as an assistant coach, he cannot help chuckling at how the game has evolved. Now, with statistical analysis opening eyes to the value of 3-pointers, no longer is the area beyond the arc the domain of smaller men.
There are few teams that better exemplify this recent shift than the Heat and the
San Antonio Spurs
, who are playing in the N.B.A. finals for the second consecutive year.
The two Miami players most likely to be found camping at the 3-point line are 6-11 and 6-10: center Chris Bosh and forward Rashard Lewis. A pivotal figure in San Antonio’s Game 1 victory was the chubby 6-8 forward Boris Diaw, who ensured that the Miami defense was stretched to the arc.
“It’s obvious it’s changed the game,” Spurs Coach Gregg Popovich said. “It makes it tougher to cover that much room defensively on the court, so you do have to pay attention to it defensively. It’s a heck of a weapon.”
Schematically, the Spurs and the Heat have little in common. Miami counts on its two best players, LeBron James and Dwyane Wade, to get into the lane and, if the defense collapses, kick the ball to the perimeter, where it can find its way to an open shooter. The Spurs, with continual cutting, screening and driving, whip the ball around in speedy syncopation that results in good looks at the rim or at the 3-point line.
Both systems work. The Heat and the Spurs are the top teams in adjusted field-goal percentage, which gives added weight to 3-point shots. It is usually a good indicator of the quality of the shots teams are taking.
In the series opener, both teams shot exceedingly well. The Spurs made 58.8 percent of their shots, including 14 of 16 in the fourth quarter, when they rallied from a 7-point deficit to win, 110-95. Miami did not shoot poorly, 47.4 percent. Combined, they made 25 of 54 3-pointers, an outstanding 46.3 percent.
Twelve players made a 3-pointer in that game.
Miami’s James Jones, a 6-8 reserve guard and former winner of the league’s 3-point shooting contest, said when he entered the N.B.A. a decade ago that he was one of the tallest outside shooters.
“It used to be Allan Houston and Reggie Miller; 6-7 wings who were shooters were an anomaly,” Jones said. “Now it’s kind of the standard for the good teams. It’s important because if you’re not making 3s or able to stretch the floor, it’s very hard to get into the paint.”

Few players in the N.B.A. exemplify this transition better than Bosh.
He grew up in Dallas, admiring Kevin Garnett — another tall, lean player who had the skills of a guard. Bosh was always an exceptional ballhandler, and he was an effective shooter in the 15- to 18-foot range. This season, that range has been extended. Bosh, who during his first 10 seasons in the league averaged 30 3-pointers per season, attempted 218 this season. He hit the game-winning 3-pointer in a playoff victory over Brooklyn.
“It’s been a challenge,” Bosh said. “It’s been a three-year transition. I know a lot of people say: ‘Ah, he needs to get down low. He needs to do this.’ I always try to sprinkle in both, and just really use my advantages and what this team needs to do. We know Dwyane and LeBron are going to be in the paint a lot, so I try to offset that as much as possible.”
That point was driven home during Bosh’s first season in Miami, when the Dallas Mavericks successfully clogged the lane while not losing track of the Heat’s few dangerous 3-point shooters. Since then, the Heat have added 3-point shooters like Ray Allen, Shane Battier and Lewis.
“Oftentimes failure gets you to that point,” Miami Coach Erik Spoelstra said. “We are not just a perimeter team. We just do it oftentimes inverted, where our perimeter players are in the paint and sometimes our bigs are outside. We had to look at our team and personnel in a different lens, and it required change.”
Popovich said he did not like the 3-point shot, but he recognized, especially after contending with the Mike D’Antoni-coached Phoenix Suns, that it could be an effective way to space the floor and prevent double teams on Tim Duncan or clogged lanes on drives by Manu Ginobili and Tony Parker.
Diaw was a key player on those Phoenix teams, a point guard in a power forward’s body.
His presence on the perimeter helped clear out space in the interior for Duncan, who was 9 for 10 and scored 21 points in Game 1. But if there is a sense that Duncan’s game is becoming anachronistic, he may be keenly aware of it, too.
From time to time, Duncan pesters Popovich about playing point guard. When he was thrown a line Saturday during a news conference — didn’t he think he should get an opportunity to run the point? — he took it like an open 3-pointer.
“I’ve been arguing that point for years now,” Duncan said. “I’m going to get your name and card, and I’ll get you in a room with him.”

Some eggplants actually do look like eggs — small, white, ovoid. Hence their name in English-speaking North America. Yet most of the world uses other monikers.
Over in Britain, they are aubergines (in France, too, of course). Italians call them melanzane, Spaniards say berenjenas. For South Asians, it is brinjal, and in the Middle East, the Arabic badinjan is the term for this ancient, luscious fruit. (It is a nightshade, like tomatoes, technically a fruit, even if we do prepare it in mostly savory ways.)
Not only are there a multitude of names, there are also seemingly endless kinds of eggplant, in all shapes and colors.
Chinese markets offer slender bright magenta footlong specimens; Japanese shops have the glossy black banana-size variety; and the medium-size pale lavender Rosa Bianca eggplants so popular in Italy are now commonplace in American farmers’ markets.
There are variegated purple-and-white stripy ones called Graffiti among the many cultivars. And we haven’t even mentioned the tiny multicolored eggplants of Southeast Asia that are no bigger than a cherry tomato. Not that there’s anything wrong with the classic larger Black Beauty type we all know. The most important thing is that eggplant be freshly picked — firm, shiny, with its calyx cap still green. This ensures the flesh will be dense and sweet, without too many seeds.
O.K., you’ve got your eggplant. Now cook. How, you say? Let me count the ways (and they’re all good).
Simple eggplant cutlets: thickish slices dipped in flour and egg and rolled in homemade bread crumbs, then shallow-fried in olive oil. Eat them plain with a sprinkle of salt and a squeeze of lemon. Or bake them topped with mozzarella and Parmesan and serve with a fresh tomato sauce or with a salad of arugula and cherry tomatoes.
Split Japanese eggplants lengthwise and grill them. Once cooked, coat the cut sides generously with an unctuous miso dressing: thin some miso with a little rice wine vinegar and add a few drops of sesame oil and some grated ginger. Eat warm.
Or make a Middle Eastern smoky eggplant schmear. Grill or broil whole medium-size eggplants until the skin is charred and blackened and the eggplant is soft. Scrape away the charred skin and purée the flesh, now smoke-perfumed, with garlic, tahini and lemon juice. Add enough cayenne to give it a kick. Serve it anointed with olive oil, toasted cumin, parsley and mint, and a basket of
warm pita bread
.
Sounds a bit like baba ghanouj? Well, maybe, but who’s complaining?

Smoky Eggplant Spread

JERUSALEM —  Israeli troops closed a significant chapter in the summer’s bloody escalation of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict on Tuesday by cornering and killing the two men they suspected of kidnapping and murdering three Israeli teenagers in June.
Israeli military officials said the two suspects,
Marwan Qawasmeh, 29, and Amer Abu Aisha, 33
, had been holed up for a week in a two-story building in the West Bank city of Hebron, and refused to surrender when Israeli special forces units surrounded the building before dawn. Lt. Col. Peter Lerner, a military spokesman, said the two men “came out shooting.” One was “killed on the spot,” he said, while the other fell back into the destroyed building, where the troops then tossed grenades.
The two men, who were affiliated with Hamas, the militant Islamist movement, were hailed as heroes at their funerals in Hebron on Tuesday afternoon. Hundreds of mourners who walked behind the white-shrouded body of Mr. Abu Aisha shouted, “Go on, Hamas, you’re our dignity, and we’re your bullets.”
Earlier in the day, Israeli forces shot and wounded a Palestinian man during a protest in Hebron in which several hundred people threw rocks and firebombs and burned tires, an Israeli military spokeswoman said.
The abduction of the Israeli teenagers and the crackdown that followed fueled tensions and intensifying violence that culminated in a seven-week battle between Israeli forces and Hamas, which dominates the Gaza Strip. The three teenagers — Naftali Fraenkel and Gilad Shaar, both 16, and Eyal Yifrach, 19 — were hitchhiking home from the yeshivas they attended in the occupied West Bank when they were kidnapped on June 12.
After their
bodies were found
18 days later under a pile of rocks in an open field not far from Hebron, three Jewish extremists
abducted a Palestinian teenager
, Muhammad Abu Khdeir, 16, in his East Jerusalem neighborhood of Shuafat,
beat him and burned him alive
as an act of retaliation.
Within days of the West Bank kidnapping, Israel blamed Hamas, whose leaders at first denied knowing anything about it. In recent weeks, though, and again on Tuesday, several Hamas officials embraced the suspected kidnappers as members of their armed wing and praised their actions, though no evidence has yet been made public showing that the men acted on Hamas’s direction.
“We are proud of you, and our people will not forget your jihad,” Hussam Bardan, a Hamas spokesman, said of Mr. Qawasmeh and Mr. Abu Aisha, in a statement circulated on social media. “You trampled the occupation’s nose in the dirt and destroyed its so-called security legend.”
Some Palestinians denounced the shootout early Tuesday as an extrajudicial assassination. The news of the killing caused a delay of several hours in the resumption of indirect talks between Israelis and the Palestinians in Cairo, on the terms for continuing the Aug. 26 cease-fire that halted the hostilities in and around Gaza.
Mr. Qawasmeh, a barber, had served several terms in Israeli prisons and was part of a huge extended family in Hebron with Hamas connections. Mr. Abu Aisha also had served prison time, and was in a coma for a time after a swimming accident in 2007.

“My kids are happy that the bad guys are gone,”
Rachel Fraenkel
, mother of Naftali and six surviving children, said in a telephone interview Tuesday. “We were worried about these two dangerous people, with weapons, having nothing to lose, being out there. It’s a relief to know that they won’t hurt any other innocent people.”
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel spoke to the parents of the murdered teenagers on Tuesday. Afterward, his office said, Mr. Netanyahu told his cabinet: “There is nothing that will take away their pain, and there is nothing that will return these amazing dear boys, but I said to them, there is accounting of justice.”
Two relatives of Mr. Qawasmeh who are suspected of assisting the kidnappers are facing trial. Three more — sons of Arafat Qawasmeh, who was arrested in July — were detained by Israeli forces during the operation Tuesday morning. Hussam Qawasmeh was
indicted this month
and is suspected of being the logistical commander of the Hamas cell responsible for the abduction. Israeli officials say he handled $60,000 that was sent in five installments from Gaza to purchase two cars, two M-16 rifles and two pistols that were used in the kidnapping.
The bodies of the teenagers were found on a hilly expanse outside Hebron owned by the Qawasmeh family. Thousands of soldiers were involved in the search, in which hundreds of Palestinians, many connected to Hamas, were arrested.
The building where the suspects were killed on Tuesday — also owned by the Qawasmeh family — sits on a hillside in an urban area of north Hebron, next to Al Rubat Mosque. It contained a carpentry workshop and several shops, including a shoe store. Colonel Lerner, the Israeli military spokesman, said troops used a tractor to breach the structure around first light on Tuesday. Hours after the confrontation ended, the smell of burned leather and iron remained strong, and the iron gates to the workshop appeared to have been sprayed with bullets.
“I came here to see the barbaric action committed by Israel,” said Ahmad Ab Laban, 50, one of several people from the neighborhood.

Hotel employees often do not spend the holidays at home with their families. They are in the travel business, after all, a year-round industry. Recently, though, some hotels have started closing their doors to give employees time off at
Christmas
.
The 177-room Adoba Hotel in Rapid City, S.D., had been through a long renovation in 2013 and its general manager, Stacie Hull, wanted to reward her employees as the year came to a close. She decided to close the hotel Dec. 24 and Dec. 25 so employees could spend time with their families. It took some calls to help the approximately 50 guests who had reserved rooms make other arrangements, but it was worth it, she said.
The closure was so well received by the staff, she said, that she blocked out those days again this year.
“We aren’t part of a chain,” said Chris Donahue, a spokesman for the hotel, “so we don’t have to follow corporate rules like staying open on
Christmas
.”
Other hotels are joining in. The ones that can afford to are generally independently owned and in markets where business drops off over the holiday.
One reason for closing at Christmas is that hotels are increasingly realizing the importance of employee satisfaction, according to Mike Oshins, a hospitality professor at Boston University. Managers recognize that happy employees result in more smiles, more problems solved and better overall service.
A hotel’s location usually dictates its ability to close, Professor Oshins said. A hotel in a college town that empties for winter break won’t disappoint many customers if it closes, he said.
“If their occupancy rate is 30 percent or less, they may as well give everyone the day off,” he said.
Closing in a tourist area, by contrast, will mean the loss of more than just one or two days of business. “When a tourist comes for a week or long weekend, they want to stay at a single property for their entire visit — they aren’t going to check in at one hotel and then leave for another property when it closes,” he said. “A hotel closed on Christmas will lose multiple days of revenue.”
Ciro Ciampi owns the Sharnbrook Hotel in Bedfordshire County, Britain, with his siblings and parents. When they opened the hotel in 2006, the family decided to close on Christmas Day, Boxing Day and New Year’s Day. At first, guests were not very understanding, Mr. Ciampi said. Now the hotel sends a message explaining the desire of the owners and staff to be home with family when declining a request for Christmas accommodations. “They are more accepting when we explain,” he said.
Although it is festive, there is an added pressure on all employees when a hotel is open on Christmas, Mr. Ciampi said. Guests expect more, he said, because they are away from home on a special occasion. “If a hotel doesn’t have the right ambiance — someone dressed as Father Christmas, gifts for the children and all the bells and whistles — they will get complaints or bad reviews online,” he said.
Hotels find different ways to accommodate their clientele. At the Arnold House, a nine-room inn on Shandelee Mountain outside Livingston Manor, N.Y., which opened in May, guests can check in on Christmas Eve and keep the hotel room on Christmas Day, but there is no official staffing on that day, and no new guests can check in on Christmas. “It was an interesting dilemma balancing the needs of staff and guests,” said Sims Foster, who owns the hotel with his wife, Kirsten.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
The hotel chef lives on the property and will provide breakfast for the guests Christmas morning. Mr. Foster said he and his wife would stop by to make sure everyone was O.K. Guests do still get charged. “We called the guests who planned to be here and learned they were all going to be off the property for most of the day, so we think it will work out fine,” Mr. Foster said.
In the rarest cases, a big hotel will close. The Amway Grand Plaza Hotel in Grand Rapids, Mich., the largest in the region with 682 rooms, will be closed on Christmas Day. So will the Downtown Courtyard by Marriott in Grand Rapids. Both are owned by Amway Corporation, headquartered in Ada, Mich.
The hotel management conducted a trial closure five years ago. “I’ve worked in hospitality a long time, " said Richard Winn, president of the Amway Hotel Corporation. “It is rare to get a holiday off. So we thought this would be a special thing to do for our associates.” The closure went smoothly, so the hotel has made it an annual event.
The Downtown Courtyard hotel is part of the Marriott franchise, so Amway Hotel Corporation had to get permission from the Marriott Corporation to close it. The Amway company also owns a J.W. Marriott nearby that will remain open, so reservation workers at the Downtown Courtyard and Amway Grand Plaza refer guests there instead. Grand Rapids is home to more corporate headquarters and universities than tourist attractions, so hotel demand does slow down significantly around the holidays.
Mr. Ciampi, of the Sharnbrook Hotel, said: “We welcome guests the other 362 days of the year and give spot-on service then. But on Christmas, I want to have my own family time.”
